Which of the following statements are true regarding the graph of the function $y=f(x)$ shown above?

I. ${lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h}=0$

II. ${lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}=-1$

III. ${lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(3+h)-f(3)}{h}=-1$
question.worked_solution:
Comparing these limits with the formula for the instantaneous rate of change

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h},
$$

we see that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h} & ={f}^{′}(0), \\ {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h} & ={f}^{′}(1), \\ {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(3+h)-f(3)}{h} & ={f}^{′}(3).\end{aligned}
$$

The function consists of three line segments. Inspecting the graph, we see that

- for $-4<x<-1$, we have ${f}^{′}(x)=-1,$

- for $-1<x<1$, we have ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$

- for $1<x<4$, we have ${f}^{′}(x)=-1,$

 The derivative does not exist at $x=\pm 1.$ So, we have  

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h} & =0, \\ {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h} & =\text{DNE}, \\ {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(3+h)-f(3)}{h} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, only statements I and III are true.
